usage: The most common way to ask someone's occupation.
nuance: 직업 is the general word for one's occupation or line of work, used when asking or stating what someone does for a living. To ask politely, say 직업이 뭐예요?, and to answer, name the job with 이에요/예요. It is more neutral and formal than the casual 무슨 일 해요? (what work do you do?).
mistakes: Confusing 직업 (occupation) with 일 (work/task); 직업 is the profession itself.
Saying 직업을 해요 to mean 'I work'; instead name the job, like 선생님이에요.

examples: I asked a staff member for directions.
nuance: 직원 means an employee or staff member, anyone who works at a company, shop, or office. You will hear it constantly in stores and offices, as in 직원한테 물어보세요 (ask a staff member). It is the plain word for a worker, while 사원 sounds more like a formal job title at the bottom rank.
mistakes: Confusing 직원 (a regular employee) with 사장 (the boss/owner).
Calling a customer a 직원; 직원 is the person who works there, not the visitor.

usage: to attend a workplace; to be employed
examples: I have a job (I go to work).
My workplace is far from home.
I'm looking for a new job.
nuance: 직장 means one's workplace or the fact of having a job, so 직장에 다니다 (literally 'attend a workplace') is the everyday way to say 'I have a job.' It focuses on the company you belong to, while 직업 focuses on the profession itself. A person with a steady job is called a 직장인.
mistakes: Mixing up 직장 (your workplace/job) with 직업 (your occupation).
Saying 직장에 가다 only for today's trip; 직장에 다니다 means being employed in general.

usage: to start as a staff member
examples: There are many staff at our company.
I joined as a staff member.
nuance: 사원 is the lowest formal job rank in a Korean company, the level a new hire starts at before 대리, 과장, and higher titles. You will hear 신입 사원 (new employee) a lot every spring when companies hire. In casual talk people often just say 직원 instead, but 사원 is the official title on the rank ladder.
mistakes: Confusing 사원 (a low-rank employee) with 사장 (the company owner).
Thinking 사원 means any worker; it specifically points to the entry-level rank.

usage: to have a lot of work
examples: I have so much work today.
nuance: 업무 means the specific work or duties you handle at a job, a bit more formal than the everyday word 일 (work/thing). You will see it in set phrases like 업무 시간 (working hours) and 업무 메일 (work email). When chatting casually with coworkers, many people still just say 일 instead of 업무.
mistakes: Using 업무 for general 'work' in casual talk where 일 is more natural.
Saying 업무를 가다; you 업무를 하다 (do work), not 'go' work.

usage: 에서 marks where an action happens.
examples: There is a meeting in the meeting room.
Is the meeting room free right now?
nuance: 회의실 is the meeting or conference room at work, made of 회의 (meeting) plus 실 (room). The same 실 ending appears in 사무실 (office) and 화장실 (restroom), so it is a useful building block. To say something happens inside it, use 회의실에서.
mistakes: Confusing 회의실 (the room) with 회의 (the meeting itself).
Using 에 instead of 에서: an action happens 회의실에서, not 회의실에.

examples: I have to tell my boss first.
nuance: 상사 is the general word for a superior at work, anyone ranked above you, whatever their exact title. You usually talk about a 상사 rather than calling them '상사' to their face; instead you use their title plus 님, like 부장님. The opposite, a worker below you, is a 부하 (subordinate).
mistakes: Calling your boss '상사님' directly; address them by title + 님, like 팀장님.
Confusing 상사 (a superior person) with 회사 (the company).

usage: Add 님 when speaking to them.
examples: A senior at work helped me a lot.
nuance: 선배 is someone senior to you who joined a school or company before you, and Koreans rely on this senior-junior relationship a lot. You add 님 to address them politely (선배님). The matching word for someone junior to you is 후배.
mistakes: Confusing 선배 (joined before you) with 후배 (joined after you).
Using 선배 for an actual boss; a 선배 is senior but not necessarily your superior.

examples: I bought my junior a coffee.
That junior is good at work.
nuance: 후배 is someone junior to you who joined a school or company after you, the opposite of 선배. In Korea a 선배 often looks after a 후배, for example by treating them to a meal. You can address them by name, since you do not need to add 님 for someone junior.
mistakes: Mixing up 후배 (junior) with 선배 (senior).
Adding 님 to 후배; the polite 님 is used for seniors, not juniors.

usage: to go on a business trip
examples: I'm going to Busan on a business trip tomorrow.
The manager is away on business now.
I have an overseas trip this month.
nuance: 출장 is a business trip, traveling somewhere for work, often with an overnight stay. It differs from 외근 (off-site work within the same day) because 출장 usually means a longer, farther trip. Say 출장을 가다 to go on one and 출장 중이에요 to explain that someone is away for work.
mistakes: Confusing 출장 (a business trip) with 여행 (a leisure trip).
Saying 출장을 하다 instead of the natural 출장을 가다.

usage: 보다 is the set verb here.
examples: I have a job interview tomorrow.
I prepared hard for the interview.
I'm so happy I passed the interview.
nuance: 면접 is a job interview, and the fixed verb is 보다, so 면접을 보다 literally 'see an interview' means 'have an interview.' This 보다 pattern also appears with 시험을 보다 (take an exam). After it you hope to 합격하다 (pass) rather than 떨어지다 (fail).
mistakes: Saying 면접을 하다 instead of the correct 면접을 보다.
Confusing 면접 (interview) with 시험 (a written test/exam).

examples: I submitted my resume to the company.
I wrote my work experience on the resume.
nuance: 이력서 is a resume or CV, the document listing your education and work history when you apply for a job. You 쓰다 (write) it and then 내다 (submit) it to a company. In Korea a 이력서 traditionally includes a small ID-style photo, the 이력서 사진.
mistakes: Saying 이력서를 만들다 (craft) when 쓰다 (write) is more natural.
Confusing 이력서 (resume) with 자기소개서, the longer self-introduction essay.

usage: How much is the annual salary?
examples: My salary went up a little this year.
How much is the annual salary?
nuance: 연봉 is your salary stated as a yearly total, which is how pay is normally discussed in Korea, rather than monthly. It is made of 연 (year) plus 봉 (pay). At a new job you may go through 연봉 협상 (salary negotiation), and the monthly take-home is the separate word 월급.
mistakes: Confusing 연봉 (yearly salary) with 월급 (monthly pay).
Saying 연봉이 비싸다; for a high salary use 높다, not 비싸다.

examples: I was promoted to section chief.
nuance: 승진 means moving up to a higher rank or title at work, like going from 사원 to 대리. The verb form is 승진하다, and to say which rank you moved up to, use the rank plus 으로, as in 부장으로 승진하다. When a coworker is promoted, people say 승진 축하해요.
mistakes: Confusing 승진 (a promotion in rank) with 합격 (passing an exam/interview).
Saying 승진을 받다; use 승진을 하다 or simply 승진하다.
